core: Causes: British war debt after the Seven Years'/French and Indian War (ended 1763) and the taxes that followed (Stamp Act 1765, Townshend Acts 1767, Tea Act 1773)
The grievance of 'no taxation without representation' and Enlightenment ideas of natural rights and self-government
Escalating protest: Boston Massacre (March 5, 1770) and Boston Tea Party (December 16, 1773); the Coercive/Intolerable Acts (1774)
Outbreak at Lexington and Concord (April 19, 1775) and the Declaration of Independence (adopted July 4, 1776, drafted mainly by Jefferson)

War's course in brief: Saratoga (British surrender October 17, 1777) as turning point, the French alliance (February 6, 1778), Yorktown (Cornwallis surrendered October 19, 1781), and the Treaty of Paris (September 3, 1783)
Contradictions and limits: the Declaration proclaimed 'all men are created equal' while slavery continued; Native Americans, women, and loyalists experienced the Revolution very differently
supporting: The colonists framed their protest as a defense of the rights of British subjects before demanding independence
Saratoga's role in convincing France to enter a formal alliance
The distinction between the July 4 adoption of the Declaration's text and the earlier Lee motion for independence (June 7, 1776)
outOfScope: The wider world Age of Revolutions (French, Haitian, Latin American) — separate topic history:foundations:revolutions
The U.S. Constitution and the government that followed — separate topic history:foundations:constitution
Detailed military tactics and campaign-by-campaign narrative
Colonial-era society before the imperial crisis — history:foundations:colonial-america

claims.claim: Britain accumulated heavy debt in the Seven Years'/French and Indian War, which ended in 1763, and afterward taxed the colonies to help pay for imperial defense and administration.
Parliament passed the Stamp Act in 1765; colonial protest produced the slogan 'no taxation without representation.'
The Townshend Acts were passed in 1767, and conflict turned deadly in the Boston Massacre on March 5, 1770.
The Tea Act of 1773 provoked the Boston Tea Party on December 16, 1773; Parliament responded in early 1774 with the Coercive (Intolerable) Acts.
The first shots of the Revolutionary War were fired at Lexington and Concord on April 19, 1775.

Congress assigned the drafting of a declaration of independence to Thomas Jefferson; the final text was adopted on July 4, 1776. Richard Henry Lee had introduced the motion for independence on June 7, 1776.
The Declaration states 'that all men are created equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights.'
At Saratoga, Burgoyne surrendered about five thousand soldiers on October 17, 1777; the victory was decisive in bringing France into the war.
France signed a Treaty of Alliance and a Treaty of Amity and Commerce with the United States on February 6, 1778.
Lord Cornwallis surrendered at Yorktown on October 19, 1781, after a siege in October 1781.
The Treaty of Paris was signed on September 3, 1783, ending the war and recognizing American independence.
The Revolution's proclaimed equality coexisted with the continuation of slavery, and Native Americans, women, and loyalists experienced the Revolution very differently from the patriot leadership.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which date marks 'independence' — July 2 or July 4, 1776.
positions: Congress voted to approve independence (the Lee resolution) on July 2, 1776
Congress adopted the final wording of the Declaration on July 4, 1776, the date printed on the document
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses July 4, 1776 for the adoption of the Declaration's text (confirmed by the National Archives and the State Department Office of the Historian) and notes Lee's motion of June 7. It does not assert the July 2 vote date because the two Tier A sources read emphasize June 7 and July 4.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained only generic boilerplate ('American Revolution is a foundational concept in History') with no historical content, no dates, and no sources; essentially all of it was discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced boilerplate placeholder text with sourced historical narrative, verified dates, and real vocabulary.
Added the Revolution's contradictions (slavery, exclusion of women, Native Americans, and loyalists), which the draft omitted entirely.
rightsIssues: OpenStax U.S. History is CC BY 4.0 (attribution required); prose here is original synthesis, not adapted wording.

National Archives, National Park Service, and State Department (history.state.gov) materials are U.S. federal government works in the public domain; the one short quoted phrase from the Declaration is itself public domain.

sourceRecords.title: Declaration of Independence: A Transcription / Founding Documents
sourceRecords.notes: Confirms the Declaration is dated July 4, 1776 and the text 'all men are created equal ... certain unalienable Rights, that among these are Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness.' Federal government work, public domain.

sourceRecords.title: Milestones: The Declaration of Independence, 1776
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
sourceRecords.notes: Confirms Congress assigned drafting to Thomas Jefferson (reviewed by Franklin and Adams), Richard Henry Lee's motion of June 7, 1776, and adoption of the final text on July 4, 1776.

sourceRecords.title: April 19, 1775 — Minute Man National Historical Park
sourceRecords.notes: Confirms the first shots of the Revolutionary War were fired at Lexington and Concord on April 19, 1775, triggering an eight-year war. Read via NPS search-indexed page.

sourceRecords.title: U.S. History, 5.2 The Stamp Act and the Sons and Daughters of Liberty
sourceRecords.notes: Confirms the Stamp Act (1765), the 'no taxation without representation' slogan, and references the Sugar Act of 1764. Original prose synthesized; no wording adapted.

sourceRecords.title: U.S. History, 5.3 The Townshend Acts and Colonial Protest
sourceRecords.notes: Confirms the Townshend Acts (1767) and that 'Conflict turned deadly on March 5, 1770, in a confrontation that came to be known as the Boston Massacre.'

sourceRecords.title: U.S. History, 5.4 The Destruction of the Tea and the Coercive Acts
sourceRecords.notes: Confirms the Tea Act of 1773, the Boston Tea Party on December 16 (1773), and the Coercive Acts of early 1774.

sourceRecords.title: U.S. History, 6.2 The Early Years of the Revolution
sourceRecords.notes: Confirms 'On October 17, 1777, Burgoyne surrendered his five thousand soldiers to the Continental Army' at Saratoga.

sourceRecords.title: U.S. History, 6.3 War in the South
sourceRecords.notes: Confirms the October 1781 siege of Yorktown with Cornwallis capitulating on October 19, and the Treaty of Paris signed in September 1783.

sourceRecords.title: Milestones: French Alliance, French Assistance, and European Diplomacy during the American Revolution, 1778-1782
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
sourceRecords.notes: Confirms the Treaty of Alliance and Treaty of Amity and Commerce signed February 6, 1778, and that news of the British surrender at Saratoga (December 1777) decided France in favor of the alliance.

sourceRecords.title: Milestones: Treaty of Paris, 1783
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
sourceRecords.notes: Confirms the Treaty of Paris signed September 3, 1783, ending the Revolutionary War with Britain recognizing American independence.
